recent_posts.title: Run, Right, and Fast for the Adaptive Radix Tree
recent_posts.summary: Kent Beck streams a live coding session working on an Adaptive Radix Tree (ART) implementation, jumping into an existing project rather than starting from scratch. The session covers a sorted map API with get, put, delete, and range iteration operations. Beck mentions using Augment Code as an AI coding assistant during the session.

recent_posts.title: Software Design: Tidy First?
recent_posts.summary: Kent Beck argues that AI coding assistants ("genies") produce code that is a degraded copy of mediocre training data, landing below even the typical "muddling" zone on two key axes: working features and flexibility/optionality. He frames software value along these two dimensions and observes that AI-generated code tends to score poorly on both — claiming success while producing non-functional, inflexible code. No clear solution is offered; possibilities include better training data, better prompting, or letting models develop their own incomprehensible development style. The post ends with a call for awareness of where your code currently sits on these axes.

recent_posts.title: Nobody wants AI agents, they want outcome-oriented tools
recent_posts.summary: Kent Beck reflects on using Augment Code's Intent (a multi-agent AI coding tool) while working on an adaptive radix tree in Go. He argues that nobody actually wants agents or agent swarms — what developers want is outcome-orientation: describe a goal and get an answer on feasibility and cost. The multi-agent architecture forced him to manage coordination overhead himself, defeating the purpose. He also identifies an unsolved frontier: real-time multiplayer development where multiple humans can steer AI together, not just observe it.

recent_posts.title: Kent Beck and Amelia Wattenberger on play, productivity, and AI-augmented development
recent_posts.summary: A podcast conversation between Kent Beck and Amelia Wattenberger exploring themes of play vs. productivity in software development, the shift toward AI-augmented coding where agents handle detailed work while developers focus on strategic decisions, and what skills matter most in this new era of development.

recent_posts.title: Extreme Time Value of Money: Late-stage Career Planning
recent_posts.summary: Kent Beck applies the economic concept of time value of money to late-stage career planning, arguing that as developers age, their personal discount rate becomes non-linear and eventually infinite — making long-term equity compensation (4–12 year vesting, delayed liquidity) far less valuable than it is for younger colleagues. He reflects on how mortality, and now a Parkinson's diagnosis, sharpens this calculus: a billion dollars in 30 years is worthless if you won't be alive or healthy enough to enjoy it. He advocates for financial literacy among developers and encourages thinking about how to earn sooner and defer spending, rather than sacrificing present value for speculative future gains.

recent_posts.title: Software Design: Tidy First?
recent_posts.summary: Kent Beck, creator of Extreme Programming and author of Tidy First, publicly announces his Parkinson's diagnosis. He explains the neurological progression of the disease, shares the emotional impact, and discusses how it is reshaping his personal and business priorities. He commits to continuing his work helping developers, coding projects, and his newsletter, while emphasizing the 'time value of time' — doing meaningful things sooner rather than later.

recent_posts.title: How AI coding tools reset the career advantage of experienced engineers
recent_posts.summary: Charity Majors and Kent Beck discuss how AI coding tools have rapidly upended conventional career advice for software engineers. Majors, who spent a year urging engineers to learn to code to stay relevant, found that advice became obsolete within three months. The conversation explores why experienced engineers who built careers on writing beautiful, readable code are struggling more than others, why junior developers may have an unexpected advantage in this new landscape, and what it means that everyone's knowledge baseline has effectively been reset — nobody has a head start anymore.

recent_posts.title: Why AI providers are throttling usage at the same time
recent_posts.summary: Kent Beck applies his 3X (Explore/Expand/Extract) framework to explain why major AI model providers are simultaneously throttling usage limits. He argues the bottleneck isn't chips, compute, or money — it's the investor narrative: the moment when 'trust us, it'll work out' stops being sufficient and companies must signal a path to profitability. The synchronized throttling is a coordinated signal to the same investor class at the same stage. For developers, usage caps push them toward the API tier, splitting users into casual (free/capped), developer (metered/uncapped), and squeezed power users. Beck closes with an open question: are limits a temporary bridge while supply catches up, or the start of an Extract phase where heavy AI usage becomes a premium product?

recent_posts.title: Forest Thinning
recent_posts.summary: Kent Beck recounts a proposal he developed to resolve the logger-vs-environmentalist conflict in southern Oregon by redesigning incentive structures. Instead of paying loggers for the current harvest, he proposed paying them based on the health of the forest 10 years later, converting short-term extraction incentives into long-term stewardship incentives. This would create a reinforcing loop: careful thinning leads to healthier forests, less resistance, and more logging opportunities. The deferred payment rights could be sold as financial instruments to local investors, and environmentalists could serve as auditors of forest health. Despite being invited to present the idea at a community summit, Beck passed on the opportunity. He reflects that entrenched interests often prefer staying entrenched, but that changing rules is a prerequisite for changing behavior.

recent_posts.title: Why accomplishing half your goals can mean excellent performance
recent_posts.summary: Kent Beck shares a personal story from his early days at Facebook where accomplishing only half his goals earned him an 'exceeds expectations' review. He uses this to explain the 3X framework (Explore/Expand/Extract) and the concept of P50 goals — setting targets where achieving roughly 50% is considered on-track. In exploratory phases, completing all goals signals either sandbagging or a failure to learn. Beck argues that the software industry has shifted from Extract (stable, dependency-heavy, KPI-driven) to Explore mode, requiring a fundamental rethink of how goals, dependencies, and performance are managed.

top_posts.title: Coupling and Cohesion
top_posts.summary: The post discusses the concepts of coupling and cohesion in software design and their impact on the cost of maintenance and changes in a system. It emphasizes the importance of reducing coupling and achieving balance in design.

top_posts.title: Stretching Your TDD Skills
top_posts.summary: An exercise in TDD skills, focusing on decision-making sequences and their impact on value realization, investment deferral, and overcoming blockers.

top_posts.title: Product is a Party, Not Chess
top_posts.summary: Introducing programmers to customers can yield significant benefits, such as better understanding of user needs and emotional satisfaction from seeing the impact of their work. It's important for product leaders to facilitate these interactions thoughtfully, helping programmers develop communication skills without harboring discriminatory attitudes. The piece emphasizes treating the software development process more like hosting a party than playing a game of chess.

top_posts.title: TDD is Not Hill Climbing
top_posts.summary: The post explores the analogy of TDD (Test-Driven Development) as a hill climbing algorithm and debates its validity. It discusses the constraints TDD imposes on moving between program states and assesses potential situations where TDD might struggle. The writer critiques the original argument, delving into various strategies to handle such 'stuck spots' and questions how optimal programs should be defined in the context of TDD.

top_posts.title: Software Is Bananas
top_posts.summary: The post discusses the fundamental truths and challenges of software development, emphasizing that mistakes are inevitable and often only manifest in production. Key strategies include reducing latency between decisions and feedback, making smaller incremental decisions, and investing in reversibility to manage and mitigate errors effectively.
